name: Octisalate
lead: Octisalate (octyl salicylate, 2-ethylhexyl salicylate) is an ester of salicylic acid used in sunscreens and cosmetics as a weak UVB absorber, usually added to boost SPF and to help stabilise other filters such as avobenzone and oxybenzone.[1] It is also an emollient that adds water resistance.[1] It appears in daily SPF moisturisers and foundations, which is where it connects to appearance: sun protection is how people limit sunburn and, over years, slow the sun-driven wrinkles, dark spots and sagging that make skin look older.[14]

Octisalate is one of the six active ingredients assessed in a 2020 JAMA trial of sunscreen absorption, which found that all were absorbed into the bloodstream.[2] A 2023 review of US and EU filters listed octisalate among five ingredients whose plasma levels exceeded the FDA's exposure threshold,[11] and an industry-linked 2025 review applied a mode-of-action approach to six filters including octisalate and concluded they lack carcinogenic potential.[12] Regulators in Europe have required additional endocrine-related testing, which a company contested unsuccessfully in court.[1]

paras: Octisalate is called a weak UVB absorber, though it is more stable than some alternatives, and is used to improve the performance of filters such as oxybenzone and avobenzone and to reduce their photodegradation [1]. US labels list it in SPF foundations paired with titanium dioxide and in moisturisers paired with other filters, with standard warnings to stop use if a rash occurs [3]. A photostability study compared combinations of UV filters in a sunscreen [4].

Cosmetic ingredient reviews describe ethylhexyl salicylate as used as a fragrance ingredient, sunscreen agent and UV absorber at concentrations from 0.001% to 8%.[13] Wikipedia explains the molecule's two roles: the salicylate portion absorbs ultraviolet light while the 2-ethylhexanol portion, a fatty alcohol, provides emollient and water-resistant properties.[1]

sections.h: Mechanism and place in sunscreen formulas
paras: Organic filters are generally aromatic molecules that absorb high-energy ultraviolet light and release the energy as lower-energy radiation, so less damaging UV reaches the skin.[14] SPF, introduced in 1974, measures the fraction of sunburn-producing UV that reaches skin and mainly reflects UVB protection, assuming application at 2 mg/cm2.[14] Octisalate contributes UVB absorption and is often used with UVA filters such as avobenzone; Wikipedia states that it reduces photodegradation of other ingredients.[1] A photostability study compared combinations of UV filters in a sunscreen.[4]
Wikipedia notes that it does not produce reactive oxygen species when exposed to sunlight.[1]

Sunscreen filters are regulated as over-the-counter drugs in the United States and as cosmetics in the EU, which is why fewer filters are available in the US; a 2023 review counted 17 US and 29 EU filters, with octisalate approved in both.[11][14] In 2019 the FDA began sorting filters into categories, and Wikipedia reports that, as of 2021, only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classed as generally recognised as safe and effective, with further data requested for others after absorption studies.[14] A manufacturer-side group has proposed mechanism-based data as an alternative to rodent carcinogenicity studies for six filters including octisalate.[12]

In Europe, the European Chemicals Agency decided in 2020 that a fish sexual-development test was needed because of possible endocrine activity, and Wikipedia reports that the company Symrise lost its appeal against that decision.[1] That ruling applies to octisalate and homosalate, ingredients used exclusively in sunscreens.[1]

Wikipedia cites a 2007 review finding a good safety profile for salicylates, no reactive oxygen species formation in sunlight, and minor sensitisation potential [1]. Company REACH registrations classify it as highly toxic to aquatic life and suspected of causing fetal harm, and in 2020 the European Chemicals Agency required a fish sexual-development test because of possible endocrine activity [1]. Octyl salicylate and other filters have been measured in human placental tissue and tested for in vitro endocrine activity [5], and in river and lake water in Japan [6]; reviews address endocrine disruption potential in aquatic environments [7].

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review safety assessment covering salicylates, including ethylhexyl salicylate, is the long-standing reference for these ingredients.[13] A 2023 review of UV filters found that almost all US filters have sensitization data and that most show minimal skin sensitization.[11] Mild skin irritation has been described in some individuals.[1]

Human data are limited to absorption and allergy. The 2020 JAMA randomised trial measured plasma levels of octisalate among six ingredients [2], a phase 1 registration enrolled 72 participants [8], and a 1,000-participant European photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients [9]. A 1995 study found that a high-SPF sunscreen prevented UVB-induced immunosuppression in humans, but it tested a sunscreen as a whole [10].

In the JAMA trial, 48 healthy participants were randomized to one of four sunscreen formulations (lotion, aerosol spray, non-aerosol spray or pump spray) applied at 2 mg/cm2 to 75% of body surface area, once on the first day and four times daily on days 2 to 4, with blood sampled over 21 days; plasma concentrations of the active ingredients including octisalate were measured and compared with the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold.[2] The trial measured absorption, not clinical harm, and the FDA has not concluded that these ingredients are unsafe.[14] A 2024 modelling study estimated plasma concentrations of sunscreen actives after facial application.[15]

timeline.event: SPF is introduced as a measure of sunburn protection.[14]

card.summary: A weak UVB filter used mostly to lift SPF and steady other filters; absorbed through skin in small amounts and under European endocrine testing requirements.
card.note: ECHA required endocrine-related fish testing in 2020.

quick.overview:
Octisalate is a salicylate-based sunscreen ingredient that absorbs a little UVB light. Its main job is to raise SPF and help keep other filters like avobenzone from breaking down.

Because it is a minor filter, it has far less research than headline ingredients, mostly absorption and allergy studies.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB and also acts as an emollient that adds water resistance to formulas [1].
quick.risks: A 2020 trial found it enters the bloodstream; Wikipedia says under 1% penetrates skin and sensitisation potential is minor. European regulators required endocrine-related testing; it is classed as highly toxic to aquatic life in REACH registrations [1].

chain: Octisalate absorbs UVB and steadies other filters in the formula
Sunscreen with it lowers UV reaching the skin
Less sunburn and slower photoaging such as wrinkles and dark spots
angle.text: It is a supporting ingredient in SPF products rather than something people seek out on its own. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use is discussed as a way to keep skin looking younger, and octisalate helps formulas reach their stated SPF.
